Sometimes you need to run something at build time that isn't "compile a Zig file." You might want to generate code from a schema, embed an asset at a specific offset, run a linter, or shell out to git to embed a commit hash. The build system makes all of this composable.

Running an arbitrary command

${z(`const generate = b.addSystemCommand(&.{ "python3", "scripts/codegen.py", }); generate.addArg("--output"); const generated = generate.addOutputFileArg("api.zig"); // Use the generated file as a module const api_mod = b.createModule(.{ .root_source_file = generated, .target = target, .optimize = optimize, }); root.addImport("api", api_mod);`)}

addSystemCommand runs an external program. addOutputFileArg tells the build system "this argument will become a path; the program writes its output there; you should treat the result as a build artifact." Downstream steps can depend on the output.

Running another zig executable at build time

${z(`const codegen_exe = b.addExecutable(.{ .name = "codegen", .root_module = b.createModule(.{ .root_source_file = b.path("tools/codegen.zig"), .target = b.graph.host, // run on the build machine .optimize = .Debug, }), }); const run_codegen = b.addRunArtifact(codegen_exe); run_codegen.addArg("--schema"); run_codegen.addFileArg(b.path("schema.json")); const out = run_codegen.addOutputFileArg("generated.zig");`)}

This is the canonical Zig pattern for code generation: write the generator in Zig itself, compile it for the host, and run it as a build step. The generator can depend on Zig modules, use comptime introspection, and produce typed output.

${note('b.graph.host refers to the machine running the build, regardless of what -Dtarget says for the main artifacts. This is crucial: you want code generators to run natively, not under wasm or in a cross-compile context.')}

Embedding files

${z(`// In build.zig: exe.root_module.addAnonymousImport("assets/logo.png", .{ .root_source_file = b.path("assets/logo.png"), }); // Or use @embedFile in source: const logo = @embedFile("../assets/logo.png");`)}

@embedFile reads a file at compile time and returns its contents as a []const u8. The data lives in your binary's read-only section. Good for small-to-medium assets (icons, default config, fixture data). For very large assets, ship them separately or compress at build time.

Generated Zig source

Generated code should still enter the build graph as a file artifact. That makes dependency order explicit and keeps rebuilds deterministic.

${z(`const write_files = b.addWriteFiles(); const generated = write_files.add("generated/config.zig", \\\\pub const app_name = "demo"; \\\\pub const default_port: u16 = 8080; ); const config_mod = b.createModule(.{ .root_source_file = generated, .target = target, .optimize = optimize, }); root.addImport("generated_config", config_mod);`)}

This pattern is good for simple generated constants. For larger schemas, use a real generator executable as shown above.

Embedding a git hash

${z(`const git_hash = b.run(&.{ "git", "rev-parse", "--short", "HEAD" }); const trimmed = std.mem.trim(u8, git_hash, &std.ascii.whitespace); const options = b.addOptions(); options.addOption([]const u8, "git_hash", trimmed); root.addOptions("build_info", options);`)}

In source: const info = @import("build_info"); std.debug.print("commit {s}\\\\n", .{info.git_hash});.

Custom step types

For complex one-off logic, you can implement a custom step by subclassing std.Build.Step:

${z(`const LintStep = struct { step: std.Build.Step, files: []const std.Build.LazyPath, fn create(b: *std.Build, files: []const std.Build.LazyPath) *LintStep { const self = b.allocator.create(LintStep) catch @panic("OOM"); self.* = .{ .step = std.Build.Step.init(.{ .id = .custom, .name = "lint", .owner = b, .makeFn = make, }), .files = files, }; return self; } fn make(step: *std.Build.Step, options: std.Build.Step.MakeOptions) !void { _ = options; const self: *LintStep = @fieldParentPtr("step", step); for (self.files) |path| { const real_path = path.getPath2(step.owner, step); // run linter on real_path... std.log.info("linting {s}", .{real_path}); } } };`)}

This is more code, but you get to participate in the build graph as a first-class citizen: caching, parallelism, dependency tracking. Reach for it when addSystemCommand isn't expressive enough.

Test integration: unit-test timeouts

Per-test timeouts keep long-running or stuck tests from hanging CI indefinitely:

${z(`const tests = b.addTest(.{ .root_module = b.createModule(.{ .root_source_file = b.path("src/main.zig"), .target = target, .optimize = optimize, }), }); const run_tests = b.addRunArtifact(tests); run_tests.timeout_ms = 30_000; // 30 seconds per test process const test_step = b.step("test", "Run unit tests"); test_step.dependOn(&run_tests.step);`)}

Try it: build-time asset check

Add an assets/default.json file to a project, embed it with @embedFile, and write a test that parses it. Then add a zig build check-assets step that runs only that test artifact.

This is a practical pattern: if your binary ships default templates, schemas, database update files, or certificates, the build should prove they are readable before release.

${tip('Use --verbose with zig build to see each step the build is executing. Combined with --time-report, it makes diagnosing slow builds straightforward.')}
